title: The standard traits
summary: The traits every Rust type plugs into: derivable ones (Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash, Default), Display, From and Into, TryFrom, AsRef, Drop, and operator overloading with Add, Neg, Index and friends.

sections: PR ch12 Arithmetic and Bitwise Operators

blocks.md: Much of the standard library works through traits. `println!("{}")` needs `Display`, `==` needs `PartialEq`, `+` needs `Add`, sorting needs `Ord`, `HashMap` keys need `Hash` and `Eq`. Implement these traits for your types and they work with all of that code. *Programming Rust* calls this making your types "first-class citizens".

blocks.title: Display
blocks.md: `Debug` is for programmers; `Display` is for users, and it is never derived because only you know how your type should read. Implement its `fmt` method with `write!`. Implementing `Display` also gives you `.to_string()` through the blanket impl from lesson 2.

blocks.title: From and Into

blocks.explain: `impl Into<Celsius>` in a parameter accepts anything convertible, a common API style. Implement `From`, not `Into`: you get both.

blocks.title: AsRef and Drop
blocks.md:
**`AsRef<T>`** means "can cheaply lend a `&T`". Functions use it to accept many argument types: `std::fs::read_to_string` takes `impl AsRef<Path>`, so a `&str`, a `String` and a `PathBuf` all work.

**`Drop`** runs code when a value goes out of scope: closing a file, releasing a lock, printing a message. You cannot call `drop` methods yourself; use `std::mem::drop(value)` (in the prelude as `drop`) to drop early. Chapter 15 returns to `Drop` with smart pointers.

blocks.explain: Values are dropped in reverse order of declaration at the end of their scope. `drop(c)` moves `c` into the function, which drops it right away.

blocks.title: Operator overloading
blocks.md: Operators are trait methods in disguise. `a + b` is `Add::add(a, b)`, `-a` is `Neg::neg(a)`, `a += b` is `AddAssign::add_assign(&mut a, b)`, and `v[i]` is `*Index::index(&v, i)`. All live in `std::ops`. Implement them for your own types where the meaning is obvious, such as vectors in maths, money, or matrices:

blocks.explain: `Output` is an associated type: the result of `V2 * f64` could be any type you choose. `Mul<f64>` takes the right-hand type as a generic parameter, so `V2` could also implement `Mul<V2>` separately. Deriving `Copy` lets `a` be used after `a + ...` moved it.

blocks.title: Overload only where it reads naturally
blocks.md: *Programming Rust* advises keeping operators for types where they mean what readers expect. `+` on two money values is clear; `+` that appends a user to a database is not. Comparison operators come from `PartialEq` and `PartialOrd`, usually derived.

blocks.title: A Money type that fits in
blocks.goal: Make a type first-class by implementing Display, Default, From, TryFrom, Add, Sub, Neg, AddAssign and Sum, and deriving comparisons.
blocks.behavior:
`pub struct Money { pub cents: i64 }` (derive `Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Default` is already written).
- `Display`: `"$12.30"`, `"-$0.05"`, `"$0.00"` (dollars, a dot, two-digit cents).
- `From<i64>` (whole dollars): `Money::from(3)` is 300 cents.
- `TryFrom<&str>` with `type Error = String`: parses `"12.30"`, `"-0.05"` or `"7"` (no cents). Exactly two digits after a dot if a dot is present. Anything else gives `Err(format!("bad amount: {s}"))`.
- `Add`, `Sub`, `Neg` (all `Output = Money`) and `AddAssign`.
- `std::iter::Sum` so `vec_of_money.into_iter().sum::<Money>()` works: `fn sum<I: Iterator<Item = Money>>(iter: I) -> Money`.
hints: Display: `let sign = if self.cents < 0 { "-" } else { "" }; let c = self.cents.abs(); write!(f, "{sign}${}.{:02}", c / 100, c % 100)`.
TryFrom: strip a leading `-` with `strip_prefix`, then `split_once('.')`. Check the cents part has length 2 and all digits; parse dollars as `i64` with `.map_err(|_| err())?`.
blocks.solution_explain: Storing cents in an `i64` avoids floating-point rounding, which is why money is almost never an `f64`. Each trait plugs `Money` into a piece of the language or standard library: formatting, conversions, operators, and `Iterator::sum`.

questions.q: Why can't a struct with a `String` field derive `Copy`?
options: Copy is only for types with no heap data to duplicate; a String owns heap memory
questions.explanation: A bitwise copy would make two owners of one heap buffer.

points: Derive `Debug`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, `Hash` and `Default` when they make sense.
Implement `Display` by hand for user-facing output; it gives `to_string()` too.
Implement `From` (and get `Into`); use `TryFrom` for fallible conversions.
`AsRef` lets functions accept many argument types; `Drop` runs cleanup at end of scope.
Operators come from `std::ops` traits like `Add`, `Neg`, `AddAssign` and `Index`, usually with an associated `Output` type.

terms.def: An attribute (#[derive(...)]) that generates a trait implementation from a type's fields.
The trait for user-facing formatting with {}; implemented by hand.
Infallible conversion traits; implementing From<T> for U also gives Into<U> for T.
A conversion trait that can fail, returning Result<Self, Self::Error>.
A trait whose drop method runs when a value goes out of scope.
Implementing std::ops traits so operators like + and [] work with your types.
